content.title: By the numbers: Swiatek defeats Jovic to strengthen WTA 1000 record
content.description: Iga Swiatek defeated American teenager Iva Jovic 6-1, 6-3 to reach the quarterfinals of the China Open in Beijing. The win moved Swiatek level with Serena Williams on 148 WTA 1000 main-draw victories and into her 31st quarterfinal at the level.

related.label: 'I was shaking!' Muchova edges Osaka on ninth match point in Beijing thriller
Bartunkova’s year of growth continues to pay off with a semifinal run in Beijing
São Paulo makes history with South America's first-ever WTA Coaches Workshop

content.body:
In the first career meeting between six-time Grand Slam champion Iga Swiatek of Poland and rising American teenager Iva Jovic, Swiatek advanced to the quarterfinals of the China Open in Beijing with a 6-1, 6-3 victory Wednesday.

Swiatek dominated the opening set, winning the first five games and earning two set points in the sixth game before Jovic held serve to get on the scoreboard. The Pole then held serve to close out the set on her fifth set point.

The second set began with Swiatek breaking early to take a 2-0 lead, but Jovic began finding more range and depth on her groundstrokes. The 18-year-old, ranked a career-high No. 13 in the world, broke back to level the set.

Jovic, who entered the match on a six-match winning streak after winning the Guadalajara title last month, saved two more break points in the next game to take a 3-2 lead. But Swiatek broke twice in a row to complete the victory in 1 hour, 36 minutes.

"For sure (today), I was using more of the chances that I got," Swiatek told the media after the win. "I was more proactive. Maybe changing the directions more instead of just being solid, more intense. When I needed that, I could play long rallies and be in defense, as well. Everything was working today."

Iga advances ✅ @iga_swiatek caps off an incredible showing in Beijing against Jovic! #ChinaOpen https://t.co/jsTcgEmr8y

— wta (@WTA) October 7, 2026

Here are some of the notable numbers from Swiatek's fourth-round win:

9: Swiatek now has nine wins against players ranked in the top 20 on the WTA Tour Driven by Mercedes-Benz in 2026, against eight losses. She also recorded her 35th win against a player outside the top 10 this season, against eight losses.

31: Swiatek is through to her 31st career WTA 1000 quarterfinal. Among active players, only world No. 2 Aryna Sabalenka has reached more, with 33.

36: Swiatek has 36 wins against top-15 opponents at WTA 1000 events. Among active players, only Serena Williams, with 44, and Sabalenka, with 41, have more.

126: Swiatek has now won 126 of 128 WTA 1000 matches in which she won the first set. Both those losses have come in 2026 - to Maria Sakkari in Doha and to Magda Linette in Miami.

148: The victory was Swiatek's 148th WTA 1000 main-draw win, moving her level with Serena Williams. Among active players, only Sabalenka, with 156, has more. Overall, Swiatek and Williams are tied for seventh place for most wins since the WTA 1000 format was introduced in 2009.

Swiatek will face No. 13 seed Elise Mertens in the quarterfinals. Mertens, who defeated No. 3 seed Coco Gauff 6-3, 6-3 in another fourth-round clash on Tuesday, has not beaten Swiatek in their two previous meetings.

"I feel like my game has improved," Swiatek said reflecting on her recent form. "Obviously sometimes playing the tournament is a bit tricky. Not everything is depending on you. I believe what I'm doing makes sense moving forward.

"That gives me the most confidence. For sure when you have great results on a match, it's always a good boost of confidence. But tennis is tough. You need to be ready for every match. Your previous results are not going to give you anything. I'm going to push no matter what and we'll see how it goes."

content.title: Alexandra Eala steps out in Chanel at Paris Fashion Week
content.description: Alexandra Eala continues to make the fashion show rounds, this time appearing at the Chanel Spring/Summer 2027 show, part of Paris Fashion Week.

related.label: Week in review: Top seeds fall and a barrage of breakthroughs in Beijing
'I was shaking!' Muchova edges Osaka on ninth match point in Beijing thriller

content.body:
Alexandra Eala's star, and influence, continues to rise off the court, on all corners of the globe.

The most recent example was this week in France, where Eala attended the Chanel Spring/Summer 2027 show, part of Paris Fashion Week.

Eala, who won her first WTA Tour Driven by Mercedes-Benz title in Washington, D.C. this past summer, stepped out in a Chanel tweed jacket over a black shirt. Dark pants complemented the fit.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Alexandra Eala (@alex.eala)

"It's so surreal to experience the collection, to experience Chanel in Paris," Eala told Vogue Philippines. "I wouldn't have had it any other way for my first show."

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Vogue Philippines (@voguephilippines)

Eala's Paris Fashion Week debut comes a little under a month after appearing in several shows during New York Fashion Week. After the US Open, she attended the Tory Burch Spring/Summer 2027 showcase, where she mingled with actress Amanda Seyfried, singer Lauryn Hill and former Vogue editor-in-chief Anna Wintour. 

Eala was also spotted in the front row at Michael Kors' Spring/Summer 2027 soiree, held at The Museum of Modern Art's Sculpture Garden, and closed out her Fashion Week festivities at Calvin Klein's exhibition.

"I love the twin dresses," the World No. 18 told Vogue of her favorite Chanel looks in Paris. "Very flowy. I feel like one was inspired by day, and the other by night. I also love the very structured dresses, very simple. So many details.

"I love how they blended simple silhouettes, details, and I think everything was very wearable. That's what stood out to me."

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Vogue Philippines (@voguephilippines)

Eala's start to the Asian Swing didn't go as planned, losing to then-World No. 180 Tatiana Prozorova in her opening match in Singapore. Eala let a lead slip away in the 4-6, 7-5, 6-3 defeat, in a match that went over three hours.

She'll look to rebound next week in Wuhan, the final WTA 1000 tournament of the season. She's lost her opening matches in her two previous Wuhan appearances, first to Katerina Siniakova in 2024 and then to Moyuka Uchijima last year. This will be her first time playing the tournament as a direct entrant.

content.title: Breaking down the unlikely quarterfinal matchups in Beijing
content.description: Zheng Qinwen plays Elina Svitolina, Elise Mertens takes on Iga Swiatek, Ekaterina Alexandrova faces Mirra Andreeva and Karolina Muchova squares off with Nikola Bartunkova in the China Open quarterfinals. We break all the matches down.

related.label: Zheng powers into Beijing last eight with three-set win over Charaeva
Mertens beats Gauff for first time in six meetings to make Beijing quarters
By the numbers: Swiatek defeats Jovic to strengthen WTA 1000 record

content.body:
At the season’s most recent Grand Slam, the US Open, the top five seeds reached the quarterfinals. The top four advanced to the semifinals, with the No. 1 and No. 2 seeds meeting for the title.

Beijing has gone in the other direction. At the second-to-last 1000-level event of the season on the WTA Tour Driven by Mercedes-Benz, the top two seeds are already out, and only one of the top five remains with the quarterfinals set.

Among the final eight is an unseeded home favorite, a pair of Grand Slam champions, several tried-and-true veterans and an up-and-comer having the best tournament of her career.

Here's what you need to know about the matchups ahead of the China Open quarterfinals.

Zheng Qinwen vs. [6] Elina Svitolina

First meeting

Zheng is becoming awfully familiar with three-set matches. She won four straight three-setters to reach the US Open quarterfinals, then lost another three-set match there.

The pattern has continued at her home tournament in Beijing, where all four of her matches have gone the distance. The unseeded World No. 54 has come back from a set down twice and upset No. 15 seed Anna Kalinskaya and No. 18 seed Marie Bouzkova. On Wednesday, she defeated Alina Charaeva 6-1, 2-6, 6-4.

It's been a smoother, and less physically demanding, tournament for Elina Svitolina. The sixth seed has played one fewer match after receiving a first-round bye, and has won six consecutive sets with ease after dropping her first to Katerina Siniakova last week.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by WTA (@wta)

Surprisingly, despite both players being veterans with a track record of success, this will be their first career meeting. Zheng will surely be buoyed by her home crowd as she looks to make her first semifinal since June 2025, at Queen's Club. Svitolina most recently made the semis in Toronto, in August, and is in pursuit of her third title of the year.

[13] Elise Mertens vs. [8] Iga Swiatek

Swiatek leads the head-to-head 2-0

Elise Mertens has had to work for her quarterfinal berth. Her first-round match against Katie Volynets was a doozy. Mertens was in total control, leading 6-0, 3-0, with four opportunities to take a 4-0 lead in that second set.

But before she could comprehend what went wrong, she found herself down a break in the third. She rallied to win that match 6-0, 4-6, 7-5 in just under three hours. The World No. 19 bore down late in her next match as well, coming from 2-0 down in the decider to beat Jelena Ostapenko.

Surprisingly, her most comfortable win of the tournament came on Wednesday against Coco Gauff, whom she had never beaten in five tries. Mertens closed the match out strong, winning 10 of her last 11 service points and closing out the 6-3, 6-3 win with an ace.

Iga Swiatek had a close call in her second match, somehow finding a way to beat Donna Vekic after trailing 6-4, 5-2. But her fourth-round match against Iva Jovic was never in doubt, an authoritative 6-1, 6-3 win in which "everything was working," as Swiatek accurately put it.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by WTA (@wta)

Swiatek has never dropped a set to Mertens. In their lone match on hard courts, in Miami last year, Swiatek beat Mertens 7-6 (2), 6-1.

[19] Ekaterina Alexandrova vs. [4] Mirra Andreeva

Alexandrova leads the head-to-head 2-0

Ekaterina Alexandrova has pulled off a couple of big upsets in Beijing, coming from a set down against 11th seed Diana Shnaider and following that up with a commanding win over fifth-seeded Linda Noskova. Alexandrova wasn't broken against the Wimbledon champion, dropping just four games in a little over an hour.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by WTA (@wta)

She'll face a well-rested and in-form Andreeva, who lost her first set in Beijing to Yuan Yue. It's been smooth sailing since then, though. She rallied to win the next 12 games for the three-set win, the rare double bagel on the back end, then breezed past unseeded Polina Kudermetova and Daria Snigur to book her spot in the quarterfinals.

After the 6-2, 6-2 win over Snigur, Andreeva took to the practice courts -- not her choice, she clarified -- to work on returns. She'll certainly need a strong return game against Alexandrova, who hit six aces and won 88 percent of her first-serve points against Noskova.

Andreeva will be the favorite, considering her higher ranking and more recent success, but Alexandrova comes in with the confidence of a 2-0 head-to-head advantage. This will be their first meeting on hard courts, though. Alexandrova beat Andreeva in straight sets on clay last year, and beat her again on grass, in Bad Homburg, back in June. 

[7] Karolina Muchova vs. [26] Nikola Bartunkova 

First meeting

What a fun encounter this should be between two wildly talented Czechs, one an established veteran and the other a rising up-and-comer.

Karolina Muchova and Nikola Bartunkova have both taken dramatic paths to the Beijing quarterfinals. After Muchova beat Katie Boulter in straight sets, she came from a set down to knock off Liudmila Samsonova.

But that was just an appetizer for her next match, a nearly-three-hour marathon against Naomi Osaka that came down to a third-set tiebreak. Muchova was down breaks in both the first and third sets, and eventually clinched the match on her ninth match point. Her much-improved backhand let her down late in the third set, but she stayed aggressive with it, firing a backhand winner down the line to set up the ninth match point.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by WTA (@wta)

As for Bartunkova, she's fresh off the biggest win of her career, a 6-4, 6-3 upset of second-seeded Aryna Sabalenka. She then avoided the post-upset hangover, beating Sinja Kraus 6-0, 4-6, 6-3 to book a spot in a WTA 1000 quarterfinal for the first time.

Despite their 10-year age gap, and having never played on tour, they know each others' games well. They train at the same club in Prague and are frequent practice partners. Expect plenty of finesse, touch and exceptional shot-making in this one.

content.title: Bartunkova’s year of growth continues to pay off with a semifinal run in Beijing
content.description: Nikola Bartunkova will play in her first WTA 1000 semifinal in Beijing, and is in the middle of another run that's transcended her into the top 35 over the past year.

related.label: By the numbers: Bartunkova stuns Sabalenka to reach Beijing last 16
'I was shaking!' Muchova edges Osaka on ninth match point in Beijing thriller
On verge of first WTA 1000 quarterfinal, get to know No. 118 Alina Charaeva

content.body:
Editor’s note: At the Internazionali BNL d’Italia in Rome, wtatennis.com sat down with Nikola Bartunkova in a get-to-know interview about her game-style, rise through the ranks and more.

BEIJING -- A year and a half ago, Nikola Bartunkova was ranked No. 517 in the world and playing weekly World Tennis/ITF Events in Europe. 

Eighteen months later, she’s transcended through the rankings and sits at career-high No. 34 ahead of her first WTA Tour Driven by Mercedes-Benz 1000 semifinal at the China Open, a run highlighted by her upset of World No. 2 Aryna Sabalenka in the third round. Tuesday, she defeated Sinja Kraus 6-0, 4-6, 6-3 in the Round of 16, and Thursday, she upset No. 7 seed Karolina Muchova 6-3, 6-0 in the quarterfinal. 

“It’s been an unbelievable year for me,” Bartunkova said in Beijing. “I didn’t expect before this year that I play like this and I will be here. It’s great, but just now I focus on myself, improve my game because it’s still 50-50 every match. 

“I’m still young, so I need to have more experience and this is my goal now.”

For Bartunkova, it wasn’t just one tournament that really elevated her ranking. Rather, it was the 20-year-old’s consistency from tournament-to-tournament that gradually put her in the spotlight. 

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by WTA (@wta)

Bartunkova’s first breakout came in Guadalajara last September. As a main-draw wild card, she cruised through to the semifinals, where eventual champion and current top 15 player Iva Jovic edged her out. 

Then, at the turn of the season, Bartunkova really caught tennis fans’ attention at the Australian Open in Melbourne, where she was a qualifier. 

Advancing to her first Grand Slam main draw, she upset Daria Kasatkina in the first round and then produced the tournament’s first top 10 upset in a victory over Belinda Bencic in the second round. Bencic had entered the match on a 12-match singles winning streak.

On the clay as a lucky loser in Rome, she produced a run to the Round of 16, upsetting Madison Keys in the third round. During the grass-court season, she made the final at the Birmingham 125 before narrowly losing to then-No. 1 Sabalenka in Berlin’s quarterfinals, a match she proved to herself she could compete with the best. 

Therefore, it wasn’t a surprise to her that she ousted Sabalenka in Beijing. 

“It tells that I beat a No. 1 player, and she’s a Grand Slam champion,” Bartunkova said. “In Berlin, I had a very close match with her.  I knew can play with [top players]. 

“From Berlin, I knew I could do this."

This meteoric rise can come down to the Czech’s brand of tennis, one she dubs as “unpredictable.” It’s an aggressive style of tennis, one with plenty of shot variety, and she took inspiration from Roger Federer and Carlos Alcaraz, Bartunkova said after beating Bencic in Melbourne. 

"I think my game is the same with all the players," Bartunkova said on her mixture of forehands, slices and volleys. "Sometimes [the opponent] has better movement, more faster, but my game is the same always. I try to go for volleys. I try to go more for my shots, so that's the plan."

This playstyle is what’s powered her through Beijing, and she’ll put it to the test against either Mirra Andreeva or Ekaterina Alexandrova in the final four.

content.title: 'I was shaking!' Muchova edges Osaka on ninth match point in Beijing thriller
content.description: Karolina Muchova came from a break down in both the first and third sets, then needed nine match points to get over the line against Naomi Osaka in the China Open fourth round.

related.label: Andreeva seeks first win over Alexandrova in Beijing quarterfinal
On verge of first WTA 1000 quarterfinal, get to know No. 118 Alina Charaeva
What's it like being a ball kid at the China Open? Here's what they said

content.body:
No. 7 seed Karolina Muchova came through a spectacular fourth-round tilt at the China Open on Tuesday, denying No. 12 seed Naomi Osaka from a break down in both the first and third sets and eventually sealing her ninth match point to advance 7-5, 1-6, 7-6(7) in 2 hours and 52 minutes.

Muchova, who trailed 4-1 in the opener and 3-1 in the decider, held triple-match point at 5-4 in the third set on Osaka's serve -- but was unable to take a total of five opportunities to seal victory in that game. In the ensuing tiebreak, the Czech player missed another three match points, but converted the ninth in style with a delicate backhand volley winner.

"I honestly didn't even believe I will finish the match," Muchova said in her on-court interview. "So many match points, I didn't know how many. After a match point I was like, 'OK, I'm going for it,' but then I think she always played great and steady, and didn't make mistakes -- unlike me, unfortunately! I was shaking. I'm happy that I made the last volley and it was really so close. Naomi could be standing here. It's me, and I'm really grateful for it."

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by WTA (@wta)

In the eighth edition of the pair's six-year rivalry, Muchova backed up two grass-court victories this year to improve to 5-3 overall against Osaka -- though she still trails 3-2 on outdoor hard courts. She booked her place in her fourth quarterfinal at WTA 1000 level or above this season, following her Doha title, Wimbledon final run and Miami semifinal showing. 

Here are the key takeaways from Muchova's win:

Her backhand nearly lost her the match ... but ultimately won it for her

In previous seasons, Muchova's drive backhand has been an area of vulnerability for her -- both more prone to breaking down and less lethal than her forehand wing. She's levelled up on that side in 2026, one of the reasons this has been the most consistent of her career to date.

But as she tried to close Osaka out, it nearly let her down again. She squandered three of the five match points she held at 5-4 with backhand unforced errors -- Osaka saved the other two with an ace and a service winner. Another backhand sprayed wide enabled Osaka to hold that game, and another dumped in the net wasted her seventh match point. (Match points six and eight were lost on forehand unforced errors.)

No wonder that, at 7-7 in the tiebreak, Osaka began targeting that wing exclusively -- and nor did the 2019 champion hold back as she pummelled it at full force. Muchova managed to withstand all the pace, though -- and then find the space she needed to redirect it for a winner down the line to bring up her ninth and final match point.

"I think I was solid from the backhand side today," Muchova said. "I feel like all the players are hitting to my backhand side. But I'd say it was a shot that won the match for me today."

Muchova remains perfect in third-set tiebreaks this year

The result extended Muchova's record in third-set tiebreaks this year to a perfect 3-0 -- she also edged Ajla Tomljanovic 4-6, 6-1, 7-6(5) in the Brisbane second round, her first match of the season, and then saved a match point to deny Coco Gauff 6-2, 1-6, 7-6[10] in the Wimbledon semifinals.

The only other player with a 3-0 record in deciding tiebreaks this year is Rabat champion Petra Marcinko (who won her trio against Camila Osorio in Auckland, Yelyzaveta Kotliar in Rabat and Antonia Ruzic in Eastbourne). No player has won more than three deciding tiebreaks at tour level this year; Anna Kalinskaya has also won three, but has lost two as well.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by WTA (@wta)

Muchova's strong third-set tiebreak performance isn't new -- the 30-year-old owns an 8-3 career record in them at tour level, dating back to 2019. She hasn't lost a third-set tiebreak since the second round of the 2023 Australian Open, when she fell 6-7(1), 6-2, 7-6[6] to Danielle Collins.

That's a contrast to Osaka's 2-6 career record in deciding tiebreaks. The four-time major champion has not won one since the 2019 Stuttgart quarterfinals, when she edged Donna Vekic 6-3, 4-6, 7-6(4).

In this one, Muchova acknowledged that she "got a bit lucky" -- at 6-6, Osaka hammered a forehand return crosscourt as she sought to reach match point for the first time. Muchova only just got her racquet on the ball in response -- and her forehand dribbled over the net cord for a fortuitous steal.

Muchova faces a crafty Czech in her own mold next

Next up for Muchova is an all-Czech derby against No. 26 seed Nikola Bartunkova, who backed up her third-round upset of Aryna Sabalenka with a 6-0, 4-6, 6-3 defeat of Sinja Kraus to make her first WTA 1000 quarterfinal. It'll be the first time the pair have played each other, and an intriguing matchup. The 20-year-old Bartunkova's potent blend of power and finesse has drawn plenty of comparisons with Muchova as she's risen from No. 126 at the start of the year to her current career high of No. 34.

Muchova has been aware of Bartunkova's talent for a while longer. They both train at the same club in Prague, and are frequent practise partners on tour.

"I'm not surprised it could be a Czech match," she said. "It's on every tournament, in all the rounds you can play a Czech player. It's not really surprising anymore, I would say ... I never played Niki. She is a crafty player."

content.title: Andreeva seeks first win over Alexandrova in Beijing quarterfinal
content.description: Mirra Andreeva and Ekaterina Alexandrova advanced to the China Open quarterfinals with identical 6-2, 6-2 victories in Beijing on Tuesday. The fourth-seeded Andreeva will bid for her first win over No. 19 seed Alexandrova, who has won both of their previous meetings.

related.label: Gauff pulls away late to defeat 16-year-old Sun in Beijing
Zheng holds off Bouzkova in third straight three-setter in Beijing
Swiatek rallies from 6-4, 5-2 down to beat Vekic and reach Beijing last 16

content.body:
No. 4 seed Mirra Andreeva will take on No. 19 seed Ekaterina Alexandrova in the quarterfinals of the China Open in Beijing after both players scored comfortable straight-set victories Tuesday.

Andreeva was the first to take to Centre Court in Beijing against unseeded Daria Snigur, who was playing her first round-of-16 match at a WTA 1000 event. Andreeva dropped serve only once in the 1-hour, 3-minute contest while breaking her opponent five times in her 6-2, 6-2 win.

Closes it out and advances 🔥 Mirra Andreeva defeats Snigur in straight sets to reach the quarterfinals in Beijing! #ChinaOpen https://t.co/kkrF6vgaV8

— wta (@WTA) October 6, 2026

Andreeva hit 18 winners on the day against just 15 unforced errors, while Snigur had 32 unforced errors to 17 winners.

The 19-year-old is through to the quarterfinals in Beijing for the second time in her career. She lost to Zheng Qinwen in her only other quarterfinal here in 2024. She also advances to the last eight for the 11th time on the WTA Tour Driven by Mercdes-Benz this year.

It also marked Andreeva's 48th win of the season on tour, her most in any season so far. She trails only Jessica Pegula (50) and Elena Rybakina (49) in match wins this year.

Andreeva happy with performance but heads to practice later

"I think today I was serving well," Andreeva said after the win. "I also think that I was defending well also because she's a very aggressive player. I thought being a good defender today would be good and useful. I think I did these two things the best today."

While Andreeva, who hit six aces in the match, was happy with her performance, she was back on the practice courts after the match - something which she said was her team's decision.

"Just so you know, it was not my idea. It was not up to me (smiling)," she told the media. "It's the second day in a row the team kind of caught me off guard. Conchita (her coach) told me, We have practice court eight. I'm like, Yeah, great, exciting. We just did a lot of returns because I'm going to play against the big servers, big hitters. We just did a lot of returns. I did a lot of just basic stuff to kind of clean and feel good after the match, clean my shots."

Alexandrova becomes oldest first-time quarterfinalist in Beijing

Right after Andreeva made it into the last eight, No. 19 seed Alexandrova and No. 5 seed Linda Noskova, who reached the final here last year, followed on Centre Court. Alexandrova was equally dominant, winning 6-2, 6-2 without dropping serve in the 1-hour, 6-minute contest.

Aces it out ✅ Ekaterina Alexandrova defeats Wimbledon champion Noskova in straight sets after an incredible performance! #ChinaOpen https://t.co/DhyUR7PToS

— wta (@WTA) October 6, 2026

Alexandrova is through to the last eight in Beijing for the first time in her career. At 31, she becomes the oldest player to reach her maiden quarterfinal at the China Open in the tournament's history. She also becomes the third-oldest player to reach the last eight in Beijing, after Serena Williams and Shuai Zhang.

The win puts her into her seventh WTA 1000 quarterfinal of her career and the second of the season, after Toronto. It also marks her 22nd career win over a Top 10 player, her third of the season.

"Today's match, it wasn't easy because I know Linda, she plays so well, especially this season," Alexandrova said after the match. "I knew it's going to be difficult. With the sun today at the start, it wasn't easy because it was difficult to see the ball. I think it was a pretty good match for me. Good serve, good shots. I'm overall kind of happy with the performance and I'm glad that I could finish in two sets. Just be in the quarterfinal here in Beijing, I think it's a great start for the whole Asia Swing."

Alexandrova leads Andreeva 2-0 in head-to-head

Alexandrova has played Andreeva twice before and come away the winner each time - defeating the French Open champion at Stuttgart in 2025 and Bad Homburg in 2026 - a stat that Andreeva is well aware of.

"Well, one thing I do know for sure, I didn't beat her yet (smiling)," Andreeva said, looking ahead to her next opponent. "I will try my best with Conchita to see how I play against her, what to change, try something new that I can try to bring into the match. For sure it's going to be a great, entertaining match. She's a great player. I don't know. Pretty excited to finally get that first win against her."

Meanwhile, Alexandrova prefers not to think about their head-to-head.

"I'm trying not to think about the head-to-head," she said. "When you thinking about that, it's create more tension and more pressure on yourself. It's going to be difficult, for sure. If you put even more pressure on yourself, it's probably won't help you. We played a couple times. Every match you would play, it's different. Every time is a different condition. You can have two matches before and third will be completely different than that. It's a nice statistic, but it's better not to think about it."
content.summary: Mirra Andreeva and Ekaterina Alexandrova advanced to the China Open quarterfinals with identical 6-2, 6-2 victories in Beijing on Tuesday. The fourth-seeded Andreeva will bid for her first win over No. 19 seed Alexandrova, who has won both of their previous meetings.

content.title: On verge of first WTA 1000 quarterfinal, get to know No. 118 Alina Charaeva
content.description: World No. 118 Alina Charaeva is in the middle of her best season to date, and ahead of her fourth-round showdown with Zheng Qinwen, get to know the 24-year-old from Armenia.

related.label: Charaeva upsets new World No. 1 Rybakina in Beijing second round
Gauff pulls away late to defeat 16-year-old Sun in Beijing
Zheng pays tribute to Chinese cartoon after beating Bouzkova

content.body:
BEIJING -- World No. 118 Alina Charaeva put herself on the map with an upset -- a second-round comeback win in Beijing over new World No. 1 Elena Rybakina, who was playing her first match since the US Open. 

On Monday, she defeated Sonay Kartal in a much smoother 6-4, 6-1 win to advance to the China Open fourth round and is on the verge of a spot in her first WTA 1000 quarterfinal, but will have to get through fan-favorite Chinese wild card Zheng Qinwen on Wednesday. 

"It feels pretty special because it's my first time [in a WTA 1000 fourth round] and actually the first time in Beijing as well," Charaeva said. "I'm just really happy with my work and how I've managed my emotions and mental part as well."

Following her third-round win Monday, Charaeva sat down briefly with wtatennis.com in Beijing. Get to know the 24-year-old representing Armenia:

She's been with her coach for eight years

Charaeva's coach Carlos Martinez, and they have been working today for the last eight years. Martinez owns CMC Competition, a training tennis academy near Barcelona, Spain, where Charaeva resides. 

Martinez has brought tons of experience to Charaeva, having worked with notable player Daria Kasatkina, Simona Halep, Svetlana Kuznetsova and more. 

"He's actually like my father," Charaeva joked on how long she's worked with him. "'I'm really happy we achieved this moment together because this is our dream, and he's a really nice coach."

Charaeva has never played in a Grand Slam main draw

Charaeva has played qualifiers at each of the four majors at least once, but has never advanced out of the qualifying draw.

The closest she's come was falling short in the third round of qualifying at Wimbledon a few months ago and the 2025 US Open.

Should she continue winning in Beijing and end the season on a strong note, Charaeva could find herself with a strong enough ranking to earn direct entry into the Australian Open. Currently, she's projected to surpass her career high rank of No. 108, which she obtained ahead of the US Open.

During the Asian Swing last season, Charaeva advanced to the semifinal and final of two WTA 125 events in China and was eliminated in the first round in Tokyo and Chennai.

It's been a busy season

At the beginning of the season, Charaeva was sitting just outside of the top 160.

Now, with main draw 2026 appearances in Beijing, Rouen, Madrid, Iasi, Hamburg, Cincinnati, São Paulo and Seoul in addition to a 125 title in Midland and other strong finishes at that level, Charaeva is the middle of her best season to date. 

"Of course, people say this season is when you make a big step, but I feel it was not kind of like one big step," Charaeva said. "It was a lot of years of hard work for this result. This year and last year, I was much consistent. I didn't have a lot of injuries, so that's pretty great."

Her upcoming match against Zheng will be her 60th of the season with plenty more to go -- she has a 36-23 record on the season, including notable wins over Sofia Kenin in Seoul last week, Sara Bejlek at the Birmingham 125 and Nikola Bartunkova at Madrid qualifying. 

"This season I started to compete in a higher level, compete with a better players," Charaeva added. "For me and for my coach, our mentality is when I start to compete with better players -- even if I lose or win -- this is where you get the real level of tennis.

"I'm competing, maybe losing so much [sometimes], but we're really tight with really top players. That's where I build my level and I'm really happy that it's finally paying off."

The history she's made thus far

In her win over Rybakina, Charaeva made some unique history:

Representing Armenia, she became the first Armenian player to defeat a World No. 1 since the first WTA rankings in 1975. 

Charaeva is now the second player to defeat a World No. 1 in that top player's first match holding that ranking, joining Kristina Mladenovic in Dubai 2019 -- Mladenovic defeated Naomi Osaka. 

Since the debut of the rankings in 1975, she's the lowest-ranked player to complete a comeback win over a World No. 1. 

Since 1990, Charaeva is just the third player to defeat the World No. 1 in their first match against a WTA top 10 opponent (Julie Coin, US Open 2008 and Chang Kai-Chen, Tokyo 2009).

*Stats courtesy of OptaFacts

content.title: The first-timers who won the WTA Finals: Could Andreeva or Noskova be next?
content.description: Only seven women have won the season-ending championship in their debut, a group that includes Ashleigh Barty, Serena Williams and Maria Sharapova. Can either Roland Garros champion Mirra Andreeva or Wimbledon winner Linda Noskova be next?
content.body:
Last October, Mirra Andreeva went into the final week of the WTA Finals race in eighth place, holding the last available spot but with little room to breathe. Elena Rybakina was close behind, and Jasmine Paolini was still in the mix, leaving three players to contend for the final two places in Riyadh.

That picture held into Tokyo. When the week was over, Rybakina and Paolini had captured the two berths, and Andreeva was left on the outside looking in.

That was then. This season has offered Andreeva a far less precarious view of the Race.

On Friday, Andreeva secured her place at the season-ending WTA Finals well before the late-season squeeze. The French Open champion was joined by Linda Noskova, another first-time Grand Slam winner this year after her Wimbledon title.

They will make their first WTA Finals appearances in Indian Wells alongside Rybakina and Aryna Sabalenka, the world’s top two players. 

"This year I'm just happy that I have better odds," Andreeva said. "I'm playing better. I keep earning more and more points. That's looking good."

Said Noskova: "I feel at the end of the year, it's always really important to find motivation, to find the strength -- either mental or physical. Once you can really mentally focus on just a few tournaments, give it all, hopefully I can get some great results."

A first trip to the WTA Finals has rarely come with an easy path to the title. Since the inaugural edition in 1972, only seven women have won the event in their first singles appearance. Andreeva and Noskova will arrive in Indian Wells looking to join them.

Here’s a look at the those players who won the WTA Finals in their first appearance:

2019 Ashleigh Barty

City: Shenzhen, China

Opponent in final: Def. Elina Svitolina, 6-4, 6-3

What it meant: Barty arrived in Shenzhen having already won Roland Garros, risen to No. 1 and become the first Australian to finish a season atop the rankings since Evonne Goolagong Cawley in 1976. At the WTA Finals, she had one last chance to measure that season against the seven players who had spent the year trying to catch her.

After a round-robin loss to Kiki Bertens, Barty beat Karolina Pliskova in the semifinals and defending champion Elina Svitolina in the final. The straight-set win over Svitolina was her first in six meetings and ensured she would finish 2019 as year-end No. 1.

2016 Dominika Cibulkova

City: Singapore

Opponent in final: Def. Angelique Kerber, 6-3, 6-4

What it meant: Cibulkova’s run remains one of the more unlikely title stories in WTA Finals history. She needed to win Linz to qualify for Singapore, then lost her first two round-robin matches to Angelique Kerber and Madison Keys. A win over Simona Halep kept her alive, and she made the most of the opening.

After defeating Svetlana Kuznetsova in the semifinals, Cibulkova turned the result of her first match around against Kerber, beating the World No. 1 in straight sets for the biggest title of her career. Cibulkova became only the second player in the current round-robin format to win the WTA Finals after advancing from the group stage with a 1-2 record.

2011 Petra Kvitova

City: Istanbul, Türkiye

Opponent in final: Def. Victoria Azarenka, 7-5, 4-6, 6-3

What it meant: At the start of 2011, Kvitova was outside the Top 30. By the time she reached Istanbul, the 21-year-old had won Wimbledon for her first Grand Slam title and collected six trophies, tied with world No. 1 Caroline Wozniacki for the most on tour.

Her three-set final against Victoria Azarenka was a fitting finish. Kvitova saw a 5-0 first-set lead disappear before closing it out, then recovered from losing the second set to capture the title and move to No. 2 in the rankings.

2004 Maria Sharapova

City: Los Angeles

Opponent in final: Def. Serena Williams, 4-6, 6-2, 6-4

What it meant: Sharapova’s 2004 season had already made her the sport’s newest star. At 17, she upset two-time defending champion Serena Williams to win Wimbledon, then carried a late-season run through Seoul and Tokyo into Los Angeles, where she was making her WTA Finals debut.

She and Williams met again in the final, and Sharapova rallied from a set down to win in three sets. It was the second straight notable final in which she had beaten Williams, and it completed a year in which the teenager went from intriguing prospect to one of the game’s central figures.

2001 Serena Williams

City: Munich, Germany

Opponent in final: Def. Lindsay Davenport, walkover

What it meant:  It was the showdown that never happened. Williams was 20 and seeded seventh when she arrived in Munich for her WTA Championships debut, two months after reaching the US Open final (where she lost to her sister Venus). In Munich, Williams dropped only three games against Sandrine Testud in the semifinals to reach the championship.

Davenport secured the year-end No. 1 ranking by beating Kim Clijsters in the other semifinal, but a right knee injury forced her to withdraw before facing Williams. It was the first of five WTA Finals titles Williams would win.

1974 Evonne Goolagong 

City: Los Angeles

Opponent in final: Def. Chris Evert 6-3, 6-4
 

What is meant: Goolagong’s victory in Los Angeles came at the end of a season in which she had already won the Australian Open, the first of her four titles there. In the final, she beat Chris Evert, who had entered the event as the top seed and was in the midst of a season that included a 55-match winning streak.

It was Goolagong’s first WTA Finals title, and she would beat Evert again in the 1976 final to win the event for a second time. Across a career that made her one of the defining players of the 1970s, Goolagong won 86 singles titles and 46 in doubles.

1972 Chris Evert

City: Boca Raton, Florida

Opponent in final: Def. Kerry Melville, 7-5, 6-4

What it meant: 

What it meant: 

What it meant: Evert was the first player to win the WTA Finals in her debut, helped slightly by the fact that this was the first such event. It still counts, and the 17-year-old made it count, winning all five matches without dropping a set.

The third seed came back from 3-0 down and saved set points at 5-2 in the final to beat Kerry Melville 7-5, 6-4 before a sellout crowd in Boca Raton. One family footnote: Evert’s sister Jeanne also played in the inaugural event, losing her first-round match to Margaret Court.

For Chris Evert, it was an early marker in a career that would include three WTA Finals titles and 157 singles trophies.

content.title: Zheng pays tribute to Chinese cartoon after beating Bouzkova
content.description: After being Marie Bouzkova in Beijing, her third consecutive three-set win, Zheng Qinwen did a celebratory pose inspired by Chinese cartoon "Shen Bing Xiaojiang."

related.label: Gauff pulls away late to defeat 16-year-old Sun in Beijing
What's it like being a ball kid at the China Open? Here's what they said
Zheng holds off Bouzkova in third straight three-setter in Beijing

content.body:
Zheng Qinwen has made a habit of taking the long route through Beijing.

On Monday, she came through another three-setter, beating No. 18 seed Marie Bouzkova 7-6(3), 4-6, 7-5 for her third consecutive deciding-set win of the week. Dating back to the US Open, eight of Zheng’s past nine have gone the distance. She has won seven of them.

After Bouzkova's backhand sailed wide on Zheng's second match point, the pumped-up home favorite belted out a "Let's go" and did a superhero-like pose for the fans.

After the match, there was some speculation that Zheng's pose was in reference to soccer star Cristiano Ronaldo, or perhaps the Japanese series "Sailer Moon."

Speaking to reporters, Zheng confirmed that it had nothing to do with either of those. It was actually an ode to "Shen Bing Xiaojiang" -- translated to "Shenbing Kids" -- an animated Chinese series that debuted in 2006. She watched it growing up, she explained, and fondly remembers singing the theme song ("Meng De Guang Dian").

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by WTA (@wta)

"I told my team it's a very childish cartoon," Zheng said. "That was a transformation gesture in the cartoon. My team members were making fun of me. After winning that point, I need to do something to my team ... I think people in my age might [have grown] up with that cartoon."

It's been a very productive week for Zheng, who during media day said that the China Open is like her fifth Grand Slam. On the heels of a quarterfinal run at the US Open, she's now into the fourth round in Beijing for the second time. (The first time she did it, back in 2024, she reached the semifinals.)

Next up for Zheng is Alina Charaeva, who upset World No. 1 Elena Rybakina this past weekend and is into the fourth round of a WTA 1000 for the first time.

They've played once before on the WTA Tour Driven by Mercedes-Benz, but way back in 2020. Zheng came from a set down to win that match 4-6, 6-4, 6-4 on clay in Marbella, Spain.

content.title: Gauff pulls away late to defeat 16-year-old Sun in Beijing
content.description: Coco Gauff won nine of the final 10 games to earn a 7-5, 6-1 victory over 16-year-old Sun Xinran on Monday and reach the Beijing Round of 16 for the fourth straight year. The win improved Gauff to 24-4 in her career against younger opponents.

related.label: Zheng holds off Bouzkova in third straight three-setter in Beijing
Swiatek rallies from 6-4, 5-2 down to beat Vekic and reach Beijing last 16
What's it like being a ball kid at the China Open? Here's what they said

content.body:
Coco Gauff has typically had her way against younger players, and that trend continued Monday night in Beijing, though not without a fight. The World No. 4 pulled away late, winning nine of the final 10 games to beat 16-year-old Sun Xinran 7-5, 6-1 in 1 hour, 29 minutes and advance to the Round of 16 for the fourth consecutive year.

Beijing: Scores | Order of play | Draws

Gauff has now won 24 of her 28 career matches at the WTA Tour Driven by Mercedes-Benz level against opponents younger. Her only loss to a teenager during that span came against eventual champion Victoria Mboko in Montreal in 2025.

Returning to the Round of 16 💪 @CocoGauff moves past Sun in straight sets and continues to push towards a place at WTA Finals Indian Wells! #ChinaOpen https://t.co/Ksy9n9xbLI

— wta (@WTA) October 5, 2026

Despite the result, Gauff had nothing but praise for the young Chinese standout.

"I think she's a little bit more mature than I was at 16," Gauff said in her post-match interview. "I think I got a little bit more frustrated than she did. But she's an incredible player. I knew going in it was going to be a tough match. The junior career that she's had is incredible, and obviously she's going to do great at this level.

"I think this is the first of many matches on this court and many matches that we will play against each other. I'm looking forward to the future matchups we have."

After Gauff and Sun traded six-minute service holds in the opening two games, Gauff struck first with a break at love for a 2-1 lead. Sun immediately answered with a break of her own to level at 2-2, then held for 3-2, helping set the tone for a fiercely contested opener.

Stunning tennis from 16-year-old Xinran Sun 🌟 #ChinaOpen https://t.co/IixuNcnjG2

— wta (@WTA) October 5, 2026

A critical moment came with Gauff serving to stay in the first set at 5-4. Sun appeared to hit another winner for 15-30, but the side panels flickered during the rally, forcing the point to be replayed. Gauff took the next three points to hold for 5-all.

A backhand return winner gave Gauff the break for 6-5 in the ensuing game, and she closed out the set after 58 minutes with a love hold. 

Gauff carried that momentum into the second set, winning a fourth consecutive game to seize control of the match. Sun managed to break for 3-1, but Gauff responded by taking the final three games to secure the victory and continue her success on Chinese soil.

Job done ✅ @CocoGauff defeats Sun 7-5, 6-1 to book her place in the Round of 16 in Beijing! #ChinaOpen https://t.co/9v2XIWbkLS

— wta (@WTA) October 5, 2026

Excluding team events, Gauff owns the highest career winning percentage at WTA-level tournaments in China this century, compiling a 24-3 record (88.9%).

And, as has increasingly been the case in recent months, Gauff's net play helped drive her success. She won 17 of 22 points at the net, compared with Sun's 6 of 10 mark. She also posted a positive winners-to-unforced errors ratio, striking 26 winners against 21 unforced errors.

Next up is No. 13 seed Elise Mertens, against whom Gauff owns a 5-0 career record, including a comeback victory in Dubai earlier this year.

Before turning her attention to the next round, Gauff took one final moment to reflect on her latest opponent. She even offered a player comparison for Sun, who entered the week ranked No. 582 and earned her first Top 100 and Top 50 victory against Cristina Bucsa in the second round.

"She doesn't have any major weaknesses," Gauff told reporters. "She can get a lot of balls back and play aggressive. She hits it real flat. Kind of reminds me of Jess [Pegula] a little bit. Her standout shot? I think it depends on the player. Today she was hitting her forehand line really well. Obviously she has a great backhand, too. Killed me on a couple backhand crosses."

content.title: Week in review: Top seeds fall and a barrage of breakthroughs in Beijing
content.description: Top seeds Elena Rybakina and Aryna Sabalenka went down early in Beijing, and Sun Xinran, Alina Charaeva and Nikola Bartunkova had the weeks of their careers.

related.label: 'I was shaking!' Muchova edges Osaka on ninth match point in Beijing thriller
Bartunkova’s year of growth continues to pay off with a semifinal run in Beijing
Gauff pulls away late to defeat 16-year-old Sun in Beijing

content.body:
No lead was safe during the first week of the China Open.

The same could be said for the top two seeds and presumptive favorites.

We've also seen a trio of breakthroughs in Beijing, from players who could very well be contending for titles in the not-too-distant future (if not immediately).

As the 96-player draw has begun to whittle down to eight, there have been no shortage of compelling storylines and memorable moments, and more than a few plot twists. Before the second-to-last WTA 1000 tournament of 2026 heads toward its conclusion, we reflect on the notable happenings from an eventful first week of play.

Star of the Week

Alina Charaeva

Alina Charaeva's week looked to be over before it started, as she fell behind a set and a break to Yuliia Starodubtseva in the first round. She fought her way back in that one, rallying for a 5-7, 7-5, 6-2 win in 3 hours and 12 minutes. 

That alone would have been a career highlight, as it was her first WTA 1000 win. But she followed it up with the moment of her career, knocking off World No. 1 Elena Rybakina in the second round (much more on that below). She came from a set down in that match, too.

The World No. 118 carried that momentum into her third-round match, where she had a far easier time with Sonay Kartal 6-4, 6-1.

Charaeva could make her Top 100 debut next week even if she loses her next match, though it will depend on other players' results. But defeating Zheng Qinwen in the fourth round would guarantee it.

Breakthrough of the Week

Sun Xinran

She only won two matches, but 16-year-old Sun Xinran made quite an impression in her WTA Tour Driven by Mercedes-Benz debut.

Playing in front of her home fans, the US Open girls' champion and junior World No. 1 took nine of 10 games from Eva Lys in her opener, before Lys retired with a foot injury.

In her next match, Sun upset 27th seed Cristina Bucsa 6-4, 7-5 to pick up the first Top 50 win of her young career. That set up a match against fourth-ranked Coco Gauff. Sun played her tough in the first set before Gauff pulled away for a 7-5, 6-1 win.

Afterwards, Gauff was very complimentary of the rising star.

"She's an incredible player," Gauff said. "I knew going in it was going to be a tough match. The junior career that she's had is incredible, and obviously she's going to do great at this level.

"I think this is the first of many matches on this court and many matches that we will play against each other. I'm looking forward to the future matchups we have."

Honorable mention: Nikola Bartunkova, who upset No. 2 Aryna Sabalenka and is into her first career WTA 1000 quarterfinal.

Biggest Upset of the Week

Alina Charaeva d. Elena Rybakina, second round

How big was this upset? Consider this: Only once before had a player lost her first match after securing the No. 1 ranking. Charaeva also became just the ninth player outside the Top 100 to beat a World No. 1, and the lowest-ranked player ever to beat a World No. 1 after being a set down.

It was just the 17th tour-level match of the 24-year-old Armenian's career. Prior to beating Rybakina, her best win came against then-No. 31 Wang Xinyu earlier this year.

"Of course, I was just trying to enjoy, to not be so nervous," Charaeva admitted. "It wasn't possible. I was so nervous anyway."

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by WTA (@wta)

Best Match of the Week

Elise Mertens d. Katie Volynets, second round

What an odd match this was. Elise Mertens absolutely dominated early on, taking the first nine games for a commanding 6-0, 3-0 lead. She then had four opportunities to go up 4-0 in the second, with a double bagel looking like a very real possibility.

Then Katie Volynets flipped the script abruptly. She stole the second and went up a break in the third before Mertens found her footing again, escaping with a 6-0, 4-6, 7-5 win in 2 hours and 54 minutes.

Best Comeback of the Week

Iga Swiatek d. Donna Vekic, third round

Late in her second set against Donna Vekic, Iga Swiatek appeared to be joining Sabalenka and Elena Rybakina as multiple-Slam-champion casualties in Beijing. Swiatek trailed 6-4, 5-2, but broke twice to level the match at 5-all. She then took the tiebreaker without dropping a point.

They exchanged breaks to open the decider, and after breaking again for 3-2, Swiatek took the final three games for the 4-6, 7-6 (0), 6-2 win.

Best Shot of the Week

Karolina Muchova's 360-degree pickup and pass

At 3-all in the first-set tiebreaker, Katie Boulter returned Karolina Muchova's serve just beyond the baseline. The Wimbledon runner-up responded with an improbable 360-degree spinning pickup. Boulter got to it and beautifully flicked it toward the sideline. Muchova read it, shuffled to the alley and won the point with a perfectly-angled pass.

As good, and as smooth, as it gets. Muchova won the match 7-6 (3), 6-1.

Social Moment of the Week

WTA stars take to the red carpet

Before play began in Beijing, a collection of WTA Tour Driven by Mercedes-Benz stars had the opportunity to relax, laugh and mingle at the player party.

They also showcased an array of stunning looks and styles on the red carpet. Check out all the photos here.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by WTA (@wta)

Biggest Off-Court News of the Week

Equal prize money milestone

It was a quite a busy week off the court.

The WTA was thrilled to announce that in 2027, all combined WTA 1000 events will award equal prize money for the first time. The 2027 calendar was also revealed, including a new WTA 250 tournament in Manila, Philippines. 

To read more about calendar changes and the new Tournament Investment Fund, click here.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by WTA (@wta)

Most Dominant Performance of the Week

Daria Snigur d. Taylah Preston, third round

Forty-seven minutes ...47 minutes! That's how long it took for Daria Snigur to beat Taylah Preston 6-1, 6-0 in the China Open third round.

Best Stat of the Week

Points to winners ratio

In Sabalenka's 6-1, 6-3 win over Renata Zarazua, Sabalenka hit 36 winners -- two more than Zarazua's total points won (34).

content.title: Zheng holds off Bouzkova in third straight three-setter in Beijing
content.description: Zheng Qinwen narrowly defeated Czechia's Marie Bouzkova in 2 hours and 54 minutes in her third straight three-setter in Beijing. She will next face Alina Charaeva in the Round of 16.

related.label: Swiatek rallies from 6-4, 5-2 down to beat Vekic and reach Beijing last 16
Around Beijing: Ostapenko enters influencer era as Sakkari's mindset evolves
Potapova shuts down 2026 season after Beijing retirement

content.body:
BEIJING -- Three matches in, and it's another three-setter for Zheng Qinwen. 

In a close 7-6(3), 4-6, 7-5 win over No. 18 seed Marie Bouzkova in 2 hours and 54 minutes, Zheng is through to the Round of 16 at the China Open for the first time since 2024 after her third consecutive match that went to a decider.

"I just think I believe here everybody wants to take me down," Zheng said to press. "They really show up [with] their best tennis. I believe somehow they prove that the level was really high."

She will next face Alina Charaeva, who is in the middle of an unexpected run to the fourth round after defeating Sonay Kartal Monday just days following her upset win over World No. 1 Elena Rybakina. 

Zheng, a wild card in Beijing, has now played a total of eight hours and one minute on court, the most of any player thus far the China Open, but has grinded out the win when it matters most in the deciding set. Of her 21 wins this season on the WTA Tour Driven by Mercedes-Benz, Zheng has won 13 of them in deciding sets. 

During her post-match press conference, Zheng quickly pointed to a moment when she led 3-1 in the first set that in hindsight she wished she did better mentally. On Bouzkova's serve, Zheng created a triple break opportunity, but Bouzkova ultimately held. 

MATCH FOR THE AGES ⭐️ Zheng Qinwen moves into the Round of 16 in Beijing defeating Bouzkova in a three-set thriller that we couldn’t take our eyes off! #ChinaOpen https://t.co/VR1tqKHXIv

— wta (@WTA) October 5, 2026

Before the tournament, Zheng explained how Beijing feels like her fifth Grand Slam, and that she truly wants to put on a strong outing for her home-crowd. While the Chinese crowd gives her plenty of motivation, she's trying to let the pressure build like it did in that early moment in the first set.

"Of course, I'm really happy to win because I felt like maybe [the opponent] plays without pressure, but I felt I really play with lot of pressure because I want to perform well in front of my home crowd," Zheng said. "This gives me energy, but in the same time I believe maybe I should be a bit more chill, more relax on court, especially when I'm leading 3-1 in the first set.

"Those mistakes... I believe I should [have] done it better."

Throughout the match, Zheng put pressure on Bouzkova's serve, forcing 12 break-point chances and winning 36% of Bouzkova's first-service points and 53% of her second-service points. On Zheng's serve, her 81% success rate on first-service points (46-of-57) and 11 aces might have just been the difference -- her 26 aces this tournament are the most of any player. 

Zheng said she didn't put too much of en emphasis on her serve during practice ahead of the tournament, and though she wants to see stronger results, it's been one of her biggest weapons in Beijing and she's more pleased with how she's developed the points. 

"There was some ups and downs in my practice, I thought I could have done better," Zheng said. "What makes me happy is what I did after my serve. I didn't really practice previously, but I did better in the matches. This is something I should celebrate."

Zheng has a strong opportunity to advance to the quarterfinals against Beijing debutant Charaeva, and Zheng holds a 1-0 advantage in the head-to-head -- a 4-6, 6-4, 6-4 win in Marbella, Spain six years ago. She's seen bits and pieces of Charaeva's matches, but isn't too familiar with her game and didn't recall the match in 2020.

"To be honest, I might have seen her matches, but a little bit [of an] impression of her game, not so much. [I'm] not very familiar. After this press conference I will do my homework."

content.title: Swiatek rallies from 6-4, 5-2 down to beat Vekic and reach Beijing last 16
content.description: Iga Swiatek erased a 6-4, 5-2 deficit against Donna Vekic to extend her perfect record against the Croatian and reach the China Open round of 16. The former champion won the second-set tiebreak 7-0 before completing a 4-6, 7-6(0), 6-2 comeback in 2 hours, 40 minutes.

related.label: By the numbers: Bartunkova stuns Sabalenka to reach Beijing last 16
Osaka delivers in key moments to outlast Bejlek in Beijing third round
Rybakina withdraws from Wuhan after early China Open exit

content.body:
Iga Swiatek had won all four of her previous meetings with Donna Vekic, dropping just one set. But in their China Open third-round match Monday in Beijing, No. 30 seed Vekic appeared poised to end that run after taking a 6-4, 5-2 lead.

Swiatek, the 2023 champion, refused to let the match slip away. She broke Vekic twice to level the second set at 5-5, then won the tiebreak without losing a point to force a decider.

After the players exchanged breaks to open the third set, Swiatek broke again for a 3-2 lead and closed out a 4-6, 7-6 (0), 6-2 victory in 2 hours, 40 minutes.

"For sure I was in a bad position score-wise, didn't really know after the first set what to change to play better," Swiatek told the media after the win. "Later on in the second set I was playing more brave and more aggressive, changing more down the line. At the end I think it's what changed the rhythm of the match.

"I don't know how many points we both had, but I felt like I'm playing good. I felt like we might be even, but maybe she was winning the more important points. I knew I had my opportunities; I should push a little bit more. I just needed to go level up because she played really good, used these chances that I didn't use in the first set."

Comeback complete ✅ Iga Swiatek storms back to defeat Vekic in a three-set thriller! #ChinaOpen https://t.co/l7wTbYuaWF

— wta (@WTA) October 5, 2026

For Vekic, the loss marked her third defeat to a top-10 player in 2026, having previously lost to Mirra Andreeva at the Australian Open and Jessica Pegula at Indian Wells.

Swiatek is through to the round of 16 at a WTA 1000 event for the 40th time in her career and will be bidding to win her 13th title at this level.

It was also Swiatek's 147th win at WTA 1000 events. Only Serena Williams, with 148, and Aryna Sabalenka, with 156, have more.

She moves on to face No. 10 seed Iva Jovic next. The American defeated Kamilla Rakhimova 6-1, 7-5 in another third-round battle on Monday.

content.title: What's it like being a ball kid at the China Open? Here's what they said
content.description: At this year's China Open, there are 236 ball kids that get to share the court with some of the tournament's biggest stars. Here's a glimpse into the life of a China Open ball kid.

related.label: Swiatek rallies from 6-4, 5-2 down to beat Vekic and reach Beijing last 16
Potapova shuts down 2026 season after Beijing retirement
Osaka delivers in key moments to outlast Bejlek in Beijing third round

content.body:
BEIJING -- The China Open’s ball-kid program begins well before the first ball is struck, with 250 young candidates selected through trials beginning in August before the final group is chosen after an evaluation period.

This year, that group includes 236 ball kids -- 228 from China, four from Australia through a partnership with Tennis Australia and four from France through a collaboration with Roland Garros.

"Everyday is filled with joy when they're on court. They're happy, we try to make them healthy and we try to make them enjoy the time spent in China," Chloe Rong, Senior Manager of Competition Services, said. "That's our most important job, and [as long as] they're having fun, that's our job."

Some of the tournament's top ball kids were made available to the media, and here's what they had to say:

Zhang Xinyue, 16

Zhang, of China, found out about the possibility of being a China Open ball kid online through WeChat, and she applied instantly.

She brings Grand Slam experience to this year's Beijing group, serving as a ball kid at Roland Garros in 2025, where she was grateful to make many friends. Part of the partnership with Roland Garros is that the China Open will send its top ball kids to Paris. 

"I think it's very exciting for me," Zhang said. "It's a really good memory and experience to meet people and friends all over the world and experience famous and great players in tennis."

Zhang's favorite player is Zheng Qinwen, who is into the fourth round in Beijing. She's been following Zheng's journey after her elbow injury and recovery through the 2026 season on the WTA Tour Driven by Mercedes-Benz, where the highlight was reaching the quarterfinals at the US Open out of qualifying. 

"One of my favorite Chinese players is Zheng Qinwen," Zhang said. "I'm really glad to see her come back to the court again after her injury for quite a long time. I think it's really good for her to come back to China open and perform great on the quarter."

Talon Mackenzie, 16

Mackenzie, of Australia, attended the Australian Open in Melbourne back in 2022 and instantly knew he wanted to be a ball kid. 

So, he applied for the 2023 tournament, but then did not advance through the first round of qualifications. After skipping a year, he got accepted for the 2025 Australian Open and finished that tournament working the men's singles final. 

As a result of his strong reputation, Tennis Australia selected Mackenzie and three others to work the China Open. The China Open will similar send their top ball kids to Melbourne in addition to Paris and vice versa through a similar partnership. In Beijing, the Australian and French ball kids have a badge of their flag on the side of their cap. 

"I love tennis," Mackenzie said. "It's so awesome to just be on court with these players. It's the best seat in the house. I just tell my friends that there's no better way to spend January. It's to go to the AO."

One of the highlights was being a ball kid during on of Coco Gauff's matches at this year Australian Open during her run to the semifinal, and in Beijing, he had to chance to be on court with one of his favorite players, Alex de Minaur.  

"It's so cool to see your idols playing on court," Mackenzie said. "You're so close to them, and you can hear their conversations and get an understanding of how they're playing and how they're thinking. It's such a completely different experience compared to being in the stands."

In Beijing, Mackenzie has also had the time to explore, going on a trip to the Great Wall of China and visiting Universal Studios with other ball kids.

On-site, he's enjoyed the thrilling atmosphere of the crowd and being on court during some of the entertaining matches with players the Chinese fans rally behind.  

"China definitely does not disappoint for us, especially after a massive point and the crowd's going crazy," Mackenzie said. "All of us ball kids are doing our own thing under these pressure points, and the adrenaline rush is so crazy and so exciting."

Mackenzie has aged out of the Australian Open, so Beijing presents him the opportunity to bookend his ball kid career. 

"To have one more opportunity to come out and be with the players again is really exciting, and I'm really grateful to be able to do this again," Mackenzie said.

Li Xiaoyi, 15

Li has been a ball kid for the past four years at the China Open, and feels that the tournament has improved every year. He also went to Melbourne for his first Grand Slam as part of the Tennis Australia partnership.

From both tournaments, Li has seen the subtle differences in how each event operates in terms of procedures and standards. He also has come to appreciate the exchange in cultures of the program.

" China definitely does not disappoint for us, especially after a massive point and the crowd's going crazy. All of us ball kids are doing our own thing under these pressure points, and the adrenaline rush is so crazy and so exciting. "
Talon Mackenzie -- Ball kid at the 2026 China Open

"I think there are definitely differences in technique," Li said in Mandarin. "It's a process of mutual help and mutual improvement. We can also make friends and chat with them, which I think is pretty good."

Li's favorite part of the job is seeing five-star points on court-level, and then tossing the ball to the serving player at his request. Overall, every time he gets the 45 minutes per assignment to be on court, he soaks it all in. 

"When I see those kinds of nice key shots, I also feel happy," Li said. Including when they ask me for the ball, I also get very excited. Every time I serve [as a ball kid] them, I get very excited."

Joshua Yapi, 16

Yapi is one of four representing France, and back in May and June, he served as a ball kid at Roland Garros. That was a requirement to come to Beijing, and due to his high performance, he was selected to come to China. 

It's his first time in Beijing, and he's thorough enjoying his time at the tournament. 

"I think it's a very good organization, and the complex is super big,," Yapi said in French. "I feel comfortable here, we are well supported, we have a lot of support, the supervisors are very cool with us and the other participants help us a lot, so frankly I feel very good about the [opportunity]."

Yapi gave a glimpse into the pre-match training the group undergoes ahead of their daily schedules.

They'll conduct a short warm-up before practicing their rolls from center court to the baseline and vice versa to ensure the process is smooth without any disruption.

"Off the field, we try to work on our roll technique so that everything is perfect," Yapi said. "Our rolls have to be flat, fast, and precise."

content.title: Potapova shuts down 2026 season after Beijing retirement
content.description: Anastasia Potapova has decided to cut her 2026 season short to focus on getting fully healthy for 2027. While she produced strong results in throughout the season, it wasn't a completely healthy year for the Austrian.

related.label: Osaka delivers in key moments to outlast Bejlek in Beijing third round
By the numbers: Bartunkova stuns Sabalenka to reach Beijing last 16
Noskova, Andreeva stay in control, dodge Beijing upsets

content.body:
World No. 25 Anastasia Potapova has ended her 2026 season, she announced on social media. The decision comes a few days after Potapova retired in her opening match in Beijing against Sinja Kraus with a right shoulder injury. 

"My season has to come to an end," Potapova wrote. "Unfortunately, lately my body has been giving me more and more signs that it's time to stop. For me, that's the clearest sign that I need to take a break, give my body the times it needs to recover and come back stronger.

"See you in 2027!"

In 2026, Potapova had one of her best seasons on the WTA Tour Driven by Mercedes-Benz, improving her ranking from No. 97 ahead of Linz to a season-high and current No. 25. Her clay season was among the best of any player on tour, advancing the final in Linz, the semifinals in Madrid as a lucky loser, and the fourth rounds at Rome and Roland Garros. The highlight of her season was a 4-6, 7-6(1), 6-4 win over then-defending champion Coco Gauff at the French Open third round. 

Still, it wasn't a fully healthy season for the Austrian. At the beginning of the year in Australia, she was playing with a broken finger on her non-dominant hand. After Roland Garros, she retired in her second-round match at s'Hertogenbosch vs. Zeynep Sonmez with an illness.

The next tournament in Berlin, she retired after losing the first set to Ekaterina Alexandrova in the first round with a neck injury. 

Then, at the US Open last month, amidst a three-set battle with Mirra Andreeva, Potapova fell while chasing an Andreeva forehand, injuring her left-knee and requiring a medical timeout. At the time, Potapova was serving to stay in the match down 5-3, and though she did return to play with significant taping, she was clearly hampered and Andreeva closed out the match as Potapova left in tears. 

After Beijing, she was only scheduled to play Wuhan, but will now shift her focus to getting fully healthy for 2027. Last season, she did not play any events after Beijing either.

content.title: Mirra Andreeva and Linda Noskova secure qualification for WTA Finals Indian Wells
content.description: Mirra Andreeva and Linda Noskova reached the sport’s biggest stages in 2026, and now the two young Grand Slam champions will finish the season at the WTA Finals.
content.body:
• Both players are set to make their singles debut at the event
  • Andreeva has won three titles this season, while Noskova has won two

  • Tickets are available here for this year's WTA Finals at the Indian Wells Tennis Garden

The WTA on Friday announced Mirra Andreeva and Linda Noskova -- two of the most exciting young players on the WTA Tour Driven by Mercedes-Benz -- have secured qualification for the WTA Finals Indian Wells.

Andreeva, 19, and 21-year-old Noskova are the third and fourth players to confirm their place to compete on tennis' ultimate stage in November. They join PIF WTA World No. 1 Elena Rybakina and two-time WTA Finals runner-up Aryna Sabalenka in the draw.

Both Andreeva and Noskova will make their WTA Finals singles debuts, with Andreeva having qualified in doubles alongside Diana Shnaider in 2025.

Noskova's qualification extends the Czech Republic's run of singles representation at the WTA Finals, with the country now having at least one qualifier in 13 of the past 15 editions.

Following a breakout season in 2025, Andreeva has continued her amazing form into and across 2026 to secure her first singles qualification at the WTA Finals.

This season, Andreeva won her first Grand Slam title at Roland-Garros, reached the final of the WTA 1000 Mutua Madrid Open and claimed WTA 500 titles at the Adelaide International and Upper Austria Ladies Linz.

Joining Andreeva in making her singles debut is Wimbledon champion Noskova, whose qualification is assured as she will finish the season within the Top 7 on the PIF WTA Race to the Finals Leaderboard or as a Grand Slam champion in the No. 8-20 position.

In addition to her first Grand Slam title Noskova also triumphed on grass at the WTA 500 VANDA Pharmaceuticals Berlin Tennis Open, made the semifinals at the WTA 1000 BNP Paribas Open (Indian Wells) and posted her best result at the US Open with a quarterfinal run.

The WTA Finals Indian Wells features the Top 8 singles players and doubles teams on the PIF Race to the WTA Finals Leaderboard (with the 8th spot going to the singles player and doubles team that have won a Grand Slam if ranked No.8 to No.20).

This showcases the world’s best singles players and doubles teams competing in a round-robin format with the singles champion lifting the WTA Finals Billie Jean King Trophy and the doubles champions earning the WTA Finals Martina Navratilova Trophy. The prestigious season-ending tournament celebrates the best of the WTA on and off the court, delivering an unrivalled fan experience that blends sport, entertainment, and culture.

Tickets are available here for this year's WTA Finals at the Indian Wells Tennis Garden, one of the sport's premier destinations and tournament locations.

content.title: Osaka delivers in key moments to outlast Bejlek in Beijing third round
content.description: Naomi Osaka weathered difficult conditions and a determined challenge from Sara Bejlek to earn a 7-6 (4), 6-4 victory and reach the fourth round in Beijing. Osaka converted her fifth match point and delivered in the clutch to secure the win.

related.label: By the numbers: Bartunkova stuns Sabalenka to reach Beijing last 16
Noskova, Andreeva stay in control, dodge Beijing upsets
Charaeva upsets new World No. 1 Rybakina in Beijing second round

content.body:
Naomi Osaka passed a stern test against No. 20 seed Sara Bejlek on Sunday, overcoming a determined challenge to earn a 7-6 (4), 6-4 victory and advance to the Round of 16 in Beijing for the fourth time. The former World No. 1 needed just over two hours and five match points to secure the win.

Beijing: Scores | Order of play | Draws

Osaka not only had to fend off Bejlek, but also battle difficult playing conditions that included strong winds and cold temperatures.

"I'm really happy with how I played," Osaka said in her post-match interview. "Obviously the conditions weren't amazing, but we both have to play in them, so I never try to complain [about] that. She's an incredible player, so it's nice to have pulled out a two-set victory against her."

Little separated the two players throughout the match. Bejlek held four set points in the opening set and generated nine break-point opportunities overall, but Osaka excelled in key moments to win their first career WTA Tour Driven by Mercedes-Benz meeting.

Relief 😅

A tight encounter goes the way of @naomiosaka!#ChinaOpen pic.twitter.com/4NoXlA1R2C

— wta (@WTA) October 4, 2026

Osaka also continued to prove herself as one of the tour's best front runners. She improved to 28-2 this season when winning the first set, with her only losses in those matches coming against the world's top two players: Aryna Sabalenka in Madrid and Elena Rybakina in Toronto.

Here were three keys to Osaka's third-round win:

Clutch factor

Osaka delivered in the match's biggest moments. After being broken late in the first set, she broke back as Bejlek served for the set. A few games later, while serving to force a tiebreak, Osaka saved four set points -- including one with a well-timed volley winner -- before taking four of the final five points in the tiebreak to claim the opening set after 64 minutes.

After Bejlek double-faulted to hand Osaka a break for a 4-2 lead in the second, the four-time Grand Slam champion again rose to the occasion, saving three break points with a trio of overheads to consolidate for a 5-2 advantage.

Then, after a shaky service game in which she double faulted on match point and was broken while serving for the match, Osaka regrouped. She outlasted Bejlek in a five-deuce game -- the third of the match -- to earn the decisive break and close out the victory.

Overhead mania

While Osaka is best known for her serve and powerful groundstrokes, she frequently moved forward against Bejlek. The tactic paid off, highlighted by a series of overhead winners.

She unveiled a surprise serve-and-volley early in the first set, finishing the point with one of several overhead winners before holding at love for 2-2. Later, she used a backhand volley winner to hold for 3-3.

Her most emphatic overhead came in the first-set tiebreak, when she hammered a winner to bring up the only set point she would need. The overhead also proved crucial late in the second set, helping Osaka fend off a barrage of break points to maintain control of the match.

First-serve prowess

Given her track record, it was no surprise that Osaka excelled behind her first serve despite facing nine break points.

Big serve 👊 @naomiosaka takes the opening set, 7-6(4)! #ChinaOpen https://t.co/Gc8Yr9oEax

— wta (@WTA) October 4, 2026

She landed 69% of her first serves and won 76.7% (46 of 60) of those points. That efficiency proved especially important given that she won just 37% of points behind her second serve.

Coming into the match, Osaka ranked fourth on tour in first-serve points won at 72.3%, trailing only Rybakina, Zheng Qinwen and Linda Noskova.

What's next

Osaka will face No. 7 seed Karolina Muchova next. Muchova owns a 4-3 edge in her career head-to-head against Osaka, including wins at Bad Homburg and Wimbledon this year.

"I played Muchova recently in the quarters at Wimbledon, which sucked for me, but was great for her," Osaka told reporters. "She's an amazing player. She's someone that you know is very dangerous no matter what. She could pretty much beat anybody. But I think from my end, no matter who I play I just have to focus on myself."
